claim: Search methods based on primary sequence struggle to accurately detect homology between sequences with less than 20% amino acid identity.
source: Search methods based on primary sequence struggle to accurately detect homology between sequences with less than 20% amino acid identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific literature (Rost, 1999) as indicated in the full text.

claim: Profile- and structure-based strategies extend sensitive search capabilities into the twilight zone of sequence similarity but require slow pre-processing steps.
source: Profile- and structure-based strategies extend sensitive search capabilities into this twilight zone of sequence similarity but require slow pre-processing steps.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established knowledge about profile and structure-based methods, with implicit reference to the literature.

claim: Low-dimensionality positional embeddings can be used directly in speed-optimized local search algorithms.
source: In this work, we show that low-dimensionality positional embeddings can be used directly in speed-optimized local search algorithms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by the experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: The ESM2 3B model can convert primary sequences directly into the 3D interaction (3Di) alphabet.
source: As a proof of concept, we use the ESM2 3B model to convert primary sequences directly into the 3D interaction (3Di) alphabet or amino acid profiles and use these embeddings as input to the highly optimized Foldseek, HMMER3, and HH-suite search algorithms.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Positional embeddings as small as a single byte can provide sufficient information for dramatically improved sensitivity over amino acid sequence searches without sacrificing search speed.
source: Our results suggest that positional embeddings as small as a single byte can provide sufficient information for dramatically improved sensitivity over amino acid sequence searches without sacrificing search speed.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Direct comparisons of primary sequence using BLASTP are fast and reliable but show poor ability to detect homologs with less than about 20% identity to the query.
source: Direct comparisons of primary sequence, for example using BLASTP (Camacho et al., 2009), are fast and reliable but show poor ability to detect homologs with less than about 20% identity to the query (Rost, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Camacho et al., 2009; Rost, 1999).

claim: Profile-based methods can have high computational overhead for database construction, query preparation, or both.
source: Because of their reliance on the construction of MSAs, profile-based methods can have high computational overhead for database construction, query preparation, or both.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known requirement of MSA construction for profile-based methods.

claim: Protein structure searches show higher sensitivity than sequence searches.
source: Protein structure searches also show higher sensitivity than sequence searches (Jambrich et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Jambrich et al., 2023).

claim: AlphaFold2 and ESMFold are accurate protein structure prediction programs.
source: In the past several years, accurate protein structure prediction programs such as AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) and ESMFold (Lin et al., 2023) have led to a massive increase in the size of databases of predicted protein structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original publications describing these methods (Jumper et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023).

claim: Foldseek achieves fast structure search by encoding the tertiary interactions of each amino acid in the 20-letter 3D interaction (3Di) alphabet.
source: Foldseek achieves fast structure search by encoding the tertiary interactions of each amino acid in the 20-letter 3D interaction (3Di) alphabet.
evidence: This is a description of the Foldseek method supported by citation (van Kempen et al., 2024).

claim: Foldseek can leverage optimized sequence search algorithms originally developed for amino acid sequences by using a structure alphabet of the same size as the amino acid alphabet.
source: By using a structure alphabet of the same size as the amino acid alphabet, Foldseek can leverage optimized sequence search algorithms originally developed for amino acid sequences (Steinegger and Söding, 2017; van Kempen et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the relevant literature (Steinegger and Söding, 2017; van Kempen et al., 2024).

claim: Structure search methods suffer from the computational cost of converting primary sequences to predicted structures.
source: Structure search methods suffer from some of the same drawbacks as profile-based methods, including the computational cost of converting primary sequences to predicted structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known computational requirements of structure prediction methods.

claim: Positional embeddings produced by popular protein language models usually have large dimensions such as 1024 for ProtT5-XL-U50 and 2560 for ESM-2 3B.
source: Positional embeddings produced by popular protein language models (pLMs) usually have large dimensions such as 1024 for ProtT5-XL-U50 (Elnaggar et al., 2021) and 2560 for ESM-2 3B (Lin et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original publications describing these models (Elnaggar et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023).

claim: Classification models and methods relying on sequence embeddings struggle at discriminating individual domains of multi-domain proteins.
source: Classification models and methods relying on sequence embeddings struggle at discriminating individual domains of multi-domain proteins (Bileschi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bileschi et al., 2022).

claim: Methods relying on large positional embeddings are space inefficient, and current search implementations are slow compared to other methods.
source: Methods relying on large positional embeddings are space inefficient, and current search implementations are slow compared to other methods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational properties of large embeddings and is supported by the timing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Profile HMMs and 3Di sequences are types of protein positional embeddings with dimensionality as low as 1 (3Di sequences) to about 25 (profile HMMs).
source: We recognized that profile HMMs and 3Di sequences are types of protein positional embeddings with dimensionality as low as 1 (3Di sequences) to about 25 (profile HMMs, including amino acid frequencies and state transition probabilities), that are more suitable than amino acid sequences for the task of remote homology detection.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the authors' interpretation of these representations as embeddings.

claim: ESM-2 was already pretrained on the masked language modeling task of predicting amino acid distributions at masked positions of input sequences.
source: ESM-2 was already pretrained on the masked language modeling task (Devlin et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2023) of predicting amino acid distributions at masked positions of input sequences, therefore no additional fine-tuning was necessary to induce it to produce probabilities compatible with profile HMM tools (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original publications (Devlin et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2023) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: No additional fine-tuning was necessary to induce ESM-2 to produce probabilities compatible with profile HMM tools.
source: ESM-2 was already pretrained on the masked language modeling task (Devlin et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2023) of predicting amino acid distributions at masked positions of input sequences, therefore no additional fine-tuning was necessary to induce it to produce probabilities compatible with profile HMM tools (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the pretraining of ESM-2 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Positional amino acid frequencies predicted by ESM-2 3B resembled those found in MSAs built from sequence searches.
source: Positional amino acid frequencies predicted by ESM-2 3B resembled those found in MSAs built from sequence searches; Figure 2 shows an example comparison of logos of HMM profiles (Wheeler et al., 2014) derived from the 4HBT Pfam profile and the YBGC_HELPY___14–90 sequence from the seed alignment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the visual comparison shown in Figure 2.

claim: A two-layer 1D convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained to convert positional embeddings from the last transformer layer of ESM-2 3B into 3Di sequences.
source: To produce Foldseek-compatible 3Di sequences, we trained a two-layer 1D convolutional neural network (CNN) to convert positional embeddings from the last transformer layer of ESM-2 3B into 3Di sequences, we then unfroze the last transformer layer and fine-tuned it together with the CNN.
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the training procedure.

claim: The fine-tuned model ESM-2 3B 3Di converted amino acids to 3Di with an accuracy of 64% compared to a test set of 3Di sequences derived from AlphaFold2-predicted structures.
source: The fine-tuned model, which we call ESM-2 3B 3Di (Figure 1B), converted amino acids to 3Di with an accuracy of 64% compared to a test set of 3Di sequences derived from AlphaFold2-predicted structures.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation on test data.

claim: Training and test sets were derived from a random split of the Foldseek AlphaFold2 UniProt50 dataset.
source: Training and test sets were derived from a random split of the Foldseek AlphaFold2 UniProt50 dataset (Jumper et al., 2021; van Kempen et al., 2024; Varadi et al., 2022), a reduced-redundancy subset of the UniProt AlphaFold2 structures (see Methods for details).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the data preparation procedure, supported by citations.

claim: Methods using predicted profiles showed greater accuracy than phmmer searches across all identity bins.
source: Methods using predicted profiles (Figure 3A, B) and those using predicted 3Di sequences (Figure 3C, D) both showed greater accuracy than phmmer (amino acid to amino acid) searches across all identity bins, and hmmscan (amino acid to profile HMM) searches on test sequences below 20% identity to the closest train sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Methods using predicted 3Di sequences showed greater accuracy than phmmer searches across all identity bins.
source: Methods using predicted profiles (Figure 3A, B) and those using predicted 3Di sequences (Figure 3C, D) both showed greater accuracy than phmmer (amino acid to amino acid) searches across all identity bins, and hmmscan (amino acid to profile HMM) searches on test sequences below 20% identity to the closest train sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Methods using predicted profiles showed greater accuracy than hmmscan searches on test sequences below 20% identity to the closest train sequence.
source: Methods using predicted profiles (Figure 3A, B) and those using predicted 3Di sequences (Figure 3C, D) both showed greater accuracy than phmmer (amino acid to amino acid) searches across all identity bins, and hmmscan (amino acid to profile HMM) searches on test sequences below 20% identity to the closest train sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Methods using predicted 3Di sequences showed greater accuracy than hmmscan searches on test sequences below 20% identity to the closest train sequence.
source: Methods using predicted profiles (Figure 3A, B) and those using predicted 3Di sequences (Figure 3C, D) both showed greater accuracy than phmmer (amino acid to amino acid) searches across all identity bins, and hmmscan (amino acid to profile HMM) searches on test sequences below 20% identity to the closest train sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Foldseek searches where both the queries and database consisted of 3Di sequences produced by ESM-2 3B 3Di performed the best overall of all new methods tested.
source: Foldseek searches where both the queries and database consisted of 3Di sequences produced by ESM-2 3B 3Di (Figure 3C, D, line 7) performed the best overall of all new methods tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and 3D, line 7.

claim: Running Foldseek in 3Di-only mode led to a decrease in accuracy but still outperformed phmmer across all identity bins.
source: Running Foldseek in 3Di-only mode (line 8), a 1-byte embedding, led to a decrease in accuracy but still outperformed phmmer across all identity bins, and hmmscan on bins below 20% identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 8.

claim: Running Foldseek in 3Di-only mode still outperformed hmmscan on bins below 20% identity.
source: Running Foldseek in 3Di-only mode (line 8), a 1-byte embedding, led to a decrease in accuracy but still outperformed phmmer across all identity bins, and hmmscan on bins below 20% identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 8.

claim: HMMER3 profiles created from predicted 3Di sequences performed worse than single-sequence Foldseek searches.
source: We also tried creating HMMER3 profiles from predicted 3Di sequences (line 9). These performed worse than single-sequence Foldseek searches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 9.

claim: Patching HMMER3 to use 3Di-derived background frequencies and Dirichlet priors did not improve performance.
source: Patching HMMER3 to use 3Di-derived background frequencies and Dirichlet priors (line 10) did not improve performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 10.

claim: HMMER3 runs very slowly on 3Di sequences and profiles, presumably because the prefiltering steps were not optimized with 3Di sequences in mind.
source: Furthermore, we noticed that HMMER3 runs very slowly on 3Di sequences and profiles, presumably because the prefiltering steps were not optimized with 3Di sequences in mind.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with a speculative explanation.

claim: hmmsearch using profiles built directly from the pLM probabilities had the lowest accuracy of any algorithm.
source: Curiously, hmmsearch using profiles built directly from the pLM probabilities (line 3) had the lowest accuracy of any algorithm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 3.

claim: Profiles processed with hmmbuild from HMMER3, applying HMMER3 Dirichlet priors on top of the pLM probabilities, had better family prediction accuracy than phmmer at all but the highest identity bin.
source: Nevertheless, profiles processed with hmmbuild from HMMER3, applying HMMER3 Dirichlet priors on top of the pLM probabilities (line 4), had better family prediction accuracy than phmmer at all but the highest identity bin, and accuracy on par with hmmscan at 18% identity and lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 4.

claim: Profiles processed with hmmbuild from HMMER3, applying HMMER3 Dirichlet priors on top of the pLM probabilities, had accuracy on par with hmmscan at 18% identity and lower.
source: Nevertheless, profiles processed with hmmbuild from HMMER3, applying HMMER3 Dirichlet priors on top of the pLM probabilities (line 4), had better family prediction accuracy than phmmer at all but the highest identity bin, and accuracy on par with hmmscan at 18% identity and lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, line 4.

claim: The Foldseek-based methods all performed similarly on the SCOPe40 benchmark at all three homology levels.
source: The Foldseek-based methods all performed similarly on the SCOPe40 benchmark at all three homology levels, all outperforming pLM-BLAST and far outperforming pHMMER (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Foldseek-based methods all outperformed pLM-BLAST on the SCOPe40 benchmark.
source: The Foldseek-based methods all performed similarly on the SCOPe40 benchmark at all three homology levels, all outperforming pLM-BLAST and far outperforming pHMMER (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Foldseek-based methods far outperformed pHMMER on the SCOPe40 benchmark.
source: The Foldseek-based methods all performed similarly on the SCOPe40 benchmark at all three homology levels, all outperforming pLM-BLAST and far outperforming pHMMER (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the superfamily level, AlphaFold2-predicted structures provided the best average sensitivity.
source: At the superfamily level, AlphaFold2-predicted structures provided the best average sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 3Di sequences generated by different methods could be used as queries against databases built from 3Di sequences generated by other methods, but with some degradation of sensitivity compared to searches where both query and database 3Di sequences were generated by the same method.
source: 3Di sequences generated by different methods could be used as queries against databases built from 3Di sequences generated by other methods, but with some degradation of sensitivity compared to searches where both query and database 3Di sequences were generated by the same method (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AlphaFold2 structure prediction was by far the slowest data preparation method, taking nearly 2 weeks on the authors' hardware.
source: For data preparation time, AlphaFold2 structure prediction was by far the slowest, taking nearly 2 weeks on our hardware (Methods), and ProstT5 was the fastest, converting all protein sequences to 3Di sequences in just 6 min.
evidence: This is a timing measurement from the experiments.

claim: ProstT5 was the fastest data preparation method, converting all protein sequences to 3Di sequences in just 6 min.
source: For data preparation time, AlphaFold2 structure prediction was by far the slowest, taking nearly 2 weeks on our hardware (Methods), and ProstT5 was the fastest, converting all protein sequences to 3Di sequences in just 6 min.
evidence: This is a timing measurement from the experiments.

claim: The Foldseek-based methods were the fastest for search time.
source: For search time, the Foldseek-based methods were the fastest.
evidence: This claim is supported by the timing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: pLM-BLAST was much slower than Foldseek-based methods.
source: pLM-BLAST was much slower than Foldseek-based methods, which makes sense because it is doing the same types of Smith-Waterman alignments as Foldseek, but with positional encodings more than 500 times as large.
evidence: This claim is supported by the timing data shown in Figure 4D and explained by inference about the computational requirements.

claim: pLM-BLAST is doing the same types of Smith-Waterman alignments as Foldseek, but with positional encodings more than 500 times as large.
source: pLM-BLAST was much slower than Foldseek-based methods, which makes sense because it is doing the same types of Smith-Waterman alignments as Foldseek, but with positional encodings more than 500 times as large.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of the two methods.

claim: The pre-filtering in pLM-BLAST is not enough to compensate for the slowness of the alignment step.
source: Pre-filtering is used in both methods, but evidently the pre-filtering in pLM-BLAST is not enough to compensate for the slowness of the alignment step.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed timing differences.

claim: ESM-2 3B 3Di coupled to Foldseek enabled faster and more sensitive search than pLM-BLAST.
source: Compared to other emerging methods for neural-network-driven remote homology detection, ESM-2 3B 3Di coupled to Foldseek enabled faster and more sensitive search than pLM-BLAST (Kaminski et al., 2023), and was slower but had similar sensitivity to ProstT5 (Heinzinger et al., 2023) coupled to Foldseek.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ESM-2 3B 3Di coupled to Foldseek was slower but had similar sensitivity to ProstT5 coupled to Foldseek.
source: Compared to other emerging methods for neural-network-driven remote homology detection, ESM-2 3B 3Di coupled to Foldseek enabled faster and more sensitive search than pLM-BLAST (Kaminski et al., 2023), and was slower but had similar sensitivity to ProstT5 (Heinzinger et al., 2023) coupled to Foldseek.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 3Di sequences predicted by ESM-2 3B 3Di or by ProstT5 are compatible with Foldseek searches against experimental or AlphaFold2-generated structures.
source: Furthermore, 3Di sequences predicted by ESM-2 3B 3Di or by ProstT5 seem to be compatible with Foldseek searches against experimental or AlphaFold2-generated structures (Figure 4E), enabling a sequence annotation workflow where large numbers of proteins, for example from a newly sequenced genome, can be quickly annotated with high sensitivity by pLM-based conversion to 3Di sequences followed by Foldseek search against existing databases of experimental or predicted structures, for example the protein data bank (Berman et al., 2000) or the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A 1-byte embedding (predicted 3Di sequences run in 3Di-only Foldseek searches) was among the top performing models.
source: It is significant that a 1-byte embedding, the predicted 3Di sequences run in 3Di-only Foldseek searches, was among the top performing models.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 3Di alphabet was not developed to maximize remote homology search sensitivity, but to model tertiary interactions in protein structures.
source: The 3Di alphabet was not developed to maximize remote homology search sensitivity, but to model tertiary interactions in protein structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the original purpose of the 3Di alphabet, based on knowledge of its development.

claim: Small positional embeddings optimal for local alignment could be learned directly from a differentiable alignment algorithm instead of relying on proxy tasks of amino acid or 3Di prediction.
source: In future work, small positional embeddings optimal for local alignment could be learned directly from a differentiable alignment algorithm (Petti et al., 2023) instead of relying on proxy tasks of amino acid or 3Di prediction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions, supported by citation to relevant work (Petti et al., 2023).

claim: Pfam is a set of manually curated MSAs of families of homologous protein domains.
source: Pfam (Mistry et al., 2021) is a set of manually curated MSAs of families of homologous protein domains.
evidence: This is a description of the Pfam database supported by citation (Mistry et al., 2021).

claim: Some Pfam families presumed to have a common evolutionary origin are further grouped into clans.
source: Some families presumed to have a common evolutionary origin are further grouped into clans.
evidence: This is a description of the Pfam database structure based on established knowledge.

claim: In the clustered splits, each family is divided into train and test groups such that each sequence in the test group has less than 25% identity to the most similar protein in the train group.
source: In the clustered splits, each family is divided into train and test groups such that each sequence in the test group has less than 25% identity to the most similar protein in the train group (Bileschi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark dataset supported by citation (Bileschi et al., 2022).

claim: The CNN for ESM-2 3B 3Di consists of two layers, the first layer has 2560 input channels and 300 output channels, kernel size 5, stride 1, padding 3.
source: The CNN consists of two layers, the first layer has 2560 input channels (the size of the embeddings from ESM-2 3B), and 300 output channels, kernel size 5, stride 1, padding 3.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the model architecture.

claim: The second layer of the CNN has 300 input channels and 21 output channels (one for each 3Di symbol plus a padding symbol), kernel size 5, stride 1, padding 1.
source: The second layer has 300 input channels and 21 output channels (one for each 3Di symbol plus a padding symbol), kernel size 5, stride 1, padding 1.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the model architecture.

claim: The model was trained with a weighted cross-entropy loss function using weights of 0.1 * the diagonal from 3Di substitution matrix.
source: The model was trained with a weighted cross-entropy loss function using weights of 0.1 * the diagonal from 3Di substitution matrix.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the training procedure.

claim: Training data were derived from the Foldseek AlphaFold2 UniProt50 dataset, filtered to remove sequences smaller than 120 amino acids and larger than 1000 amino acids, and split into train, validation, and test subsets, 90%:5%:5%.
source: The Foldseek database was downloaded using the Foldseek 'databases' command line program, converted into protein and 3Di fasta files, filtered to remove sequences smaller than 120 amino acids and larger than 1000 amino acids, and split into train, validation, and test subsets, 90%:5%:5% (33,924,764:1,884,709:1,884,710 sequences).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data preparation.

claim: With ESM-2 layers frozen, the CNN was trained using the AdamW optimizer with learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.001, and exponential learning rate decrease (gamma 0.98, applied every 100 batches).
source: With ESM-2 layers frozen, the CNN was trained on the task of converting amino acids to 3Di sequences using the AdamW optimizer with learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.001, and exponential learning rate decrease (gamma 0.98, applied every 100 batches).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the training procedure.

claim: Training proceeded for 1301 batches, leading to a training accuracy of about 58%.
source: Training proceeded for 1301 batches, leading to a training accuracy of about 58%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model training.

claim: After unfreezing the last transformer layer, training continued for another 24,001 batches of 10 random training sequences.
source: The last transformer layer of ESM-2 was then unfrozen and training restarted from the saved weights, with the same training parameters. Training continued for another 24,001 batches of 10 random training sequences.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the training procedure.

claim: Accuracy on the final training batch was 65%.
source: Accuracy on the final training batch was 65%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model training.

claim: Using the final trained weights, test sequences were converted to 3Di at an accuracy of 64.4%.
source: Using the final trained weights, test sequences were converted to 3Di at an accuracy of 64.4%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation on test data.

claim: The hyperparameter of seven passes over the input sequence was chosen semi-empirically.
source: The hyperparameter of seven passes over the input sequence was chosen semi-empirically.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how a parameter was selected.

claim: In the original ESM-2 pretraining, 15%, approximately 1/7, of positions were masked at each training step.
source: In addition, in the original ESM-2 pretraining, 15%, approximately 1/7, of positions were masked at each training step, so our masking of every 7th position resembles the training conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the ESM-2 pretraining procedure, based on knowledge of the original work.

claim: The SCOPe40 benchmark dataset is much smaller than the clustered Pfam dataset, 11,211 vs 1,339,083 sequences.
source: The SCOPe40 benchmark is convenient because the dataset is much smaller than the clustered Pfam dataset, 11,211 vs 1,339,083 sequences.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the sizes of the two datasets.

claim: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, for family, true positives are matches within the same family.
source: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, the criteria for true positives (TPs) vary depending on the level of classification: for family, TPs are matches within the same family; for superfamily, TPs are matches sharing the same superfamily but not the same family; and for fold, TPs are matches sharing the same fold but are not the same superfamily.
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark evaluation criteria.

claim: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, for superfamily, true positives are matches sharing the same superfamily but not the same family.
source: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, the criteria for true positives (TPs) vary depending on the level of classification: for family, TPs are matches within the same family; for superfamily, TPs are matches sharing the same superfamily but not the same family; and for fold, TPs are matches sharing the same fold but are not the same superfamily.
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark evaluation criteria.

claim: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, for fold, true positives are matches sharing the same fold but are not the same superfamily.
source: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, the criteria for true positives (TPs) vary depending on the level of classification: for family, TPs are matches within the same family; for superfamily, TPs are matches sharing the same superfamily but not the same family; and for fold, TPs are matches sharing the same fold but are not the same superfamily.
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark evaluation criteria.

claim: In the SCOPe40 benchmark, any hits from different folds (but not from different families or superfamilies) are considered false positives.
source: Any hits from different folds (but not from different families or superfamilies) are considered false positives (FPs).
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark evaluation criteria.

claim: All 11,211 proteins were used as queries for timing in the SCOPe40 benchmark.
source: All 11,211 proteins were used as queries for timing, but for sensitivity calculations, only the 3566 proteins with at least one other family member, at least one other superfamily member, and at least one other fold member were considered.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the benchmark evaluation.

claim: For sensitivity calculations in the SCOPe40 benchmark, only the 3566 proteins with at least one other family member, at least one other superfamily member, and at least one other fold member were considered.
source: All 11,211 proteins were used as queries for timing, but for sensitivity calculations, only the 3566 proteins with at least one other family member, at least one other superfamily member, and at least one other fold member were considered.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the benchmark evaluation.

claim: Foldseek considers both 3Di and amino acid sequences in its alignments.
source: Foldseek considers both 3Di and amino acid sequences in its alignments and can therefore be conceptualized as using a 2-byte embedding.
evidence: This is a description of how Foldseek works, based on knowledge of the method.

claim: Foldseek can be conceptualized as using a 2-byte embedding.
source: Foldseek considers both 3Di and amino acid sequences in its alignments and can therefore be conceptualized as using a 2-byte embedding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Foldseek method in terms of embeddings.

claim: pHMMER uses protein sequences directly and does not require a database building step.
source: pHMMER uses protein sequences directly and does not require a database building step, so database and query preparation are not needed.
evidence: This is a description of the pHMMER method based on knowledge of how it works.
